deep.reconstruction:
This page is the draft of §17 of Riemann's Inauguraldissertation (Göttingen 1851, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse'). The published Art. 17 is close to it. The surrounding pages fit: Art. 16 is the Dirichlet-principle theorem, and the next page is the continuation of Art. 17 on the multiply connected case, poles, and the geometric interpretation as conformal mapping, which leads into Art. 18–21.

Setting. T is a surface spread over the z-plane (z = x + iy) region A, here assumed simply connected. It has boundary s and area element dT. The 'Lehrsatz' of the previous article (Art. 16) says the following. Let α + iβ be a complex function on T, continuous except on lines, with finite
L(α, β) = ∫_T [(α_x − β_y)² + (α_y + β_x)²] dT.
Then there is exactly one way to add a function μ + iν such that w = (α + μ) + i(β + ν) is analytic, μ vanishes on the boundary, and ν is prescribed at one point.

Step 1 (the existence/uniqueness count). Let w = u + iv be sought on simply connected T under three conditions:
(1) u is prescribed on the boundary as a function of s. An infinitesimal change of position changes it infinitesimally of the same order, i.e. a Lipschitz-type condition; otherwise it is arbitrary.
(2) v is prescribed at one interior point.
(3) w is finite and continuous everywhere.
Claim: these conditions determine w completely.

Riemann's proof:
- Choose any a + ib on T with a = the given boundary values.
- Make it 'Lipschitz' throughout the surface, so that a change of position by dz changes a + ib by O(|dz|). Then the integrand of L is bounded and L is finite.
- Apply Art. 16 with α + iβ = a + ib. This gives an analytic w with u = a + μ = a on the boundary, and v fixed at the one point.
- Implicit step (mine): uniqueness follows because the difference of two solutions has a real part that is harmonic and vanishes on the boundary. Hence it is ≡ 0, so the imaginary part is constant, and that constant is 0 by (2).

The margin note to (2) remarks that the choice of this value is in itself unrestricted. The stated restriction only serves to cut off unnecessary complications.

Step 2 (counting). So u on the boundary is an arbitrary function of s and determines v everywhere. Conversely, v may be given at every boundary point and then determines u, up to an additive constant that Riemann leaves implicit. The freedom in the boundary values of w is therefore a one-dimensional manifold per boundary point. Complete determination requires one (real) equation per boundary point.

The equations need not each involve only one component at one point. Two generalizations are named:
(a) At each boundary point, one equation involving both u and v, whose form varies continuously with the point. This is a mixed (oblique-derivative / Riemann–Hilbert-type) boundary condition.
(b) The boundary is split into n parts. Each point of one part is associated with one definite point on each of the other n−1 parts. For each such n-tuple of points, n equations are given jointly. This is a conjugation/transmission condition linking different boundary arcs.

Step 3 (index caveat). These conditions form a continuous manifold of functional equations between arbitrary functions. Depending on their nature, they may still need restriction or supplementation by finitely many conditions on arbitrary constants. Only then is the determination of a function of z, continuous throughout the interior, both possible and complete. This is a qualitative recognition that solvability and uniqueness of such boundary problems hold only up to finitely many constants (index/defect phenomena).
errors: Not an error of the page itself but of the underlying method: Art. 16 rests on the Dirichlet principle (existence of a minimizer). That was not justified in Riemann's time (Weierstrass's critique, 1870). It was made rigorous only by Hilbert (1900) and later work.

'Was immer möglich sein wird' is asserted without proof. The claim is that boundary data of Lipschitz type can always be extended to the interior with bounded difference quotients, hence finite Dirichlet integral. This is true for reasonable (e.g. smooth or Lipschitz) boundaries but is not argued. For merely continuous boundary data the Dirichlet integral can be infinite (Prym 1871, Hadamard), which is why the Lipschitz-type restriction in (1) matters.

The converse 'v may be given at every boundary point, whence u follows' determines u only up to an additive real constant. The page does not mention this constant. It is the counterpart of condition (2).

For the general mixed and conjugation conditions, the claim that one equation per boundary point gives a determinate problem is heuristic dimension counting. Riemann explicitly hedges this by allowing finitely many extra or fewer constant conditions. The exact count is the index of the Riemann–Hilbert problem, determined much later (Noether, Gakhov, Muskhelishvili, Vekua).

results.what: On a simply connected domain, an analytic function is uniquely determined by its real part on the boundary (Lipschitz-type data) plus the value of the imaginary part at one point; proved via the Dirichlet-principle theorem of Art. 16.
results.modern_name: Dirichlet problem for harmonic functions / Schwarz problem with harmonic conjugate normalization
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1851 (Dirichlet principle named by Riemann after Dirichlet; also Gauss, Green, Thomson); Schwarz for rigorous solution on the disc (1870)

results.what: Counting principle: boundary data of w carry one real degree of freedom per boundary point, so one real equation per boundary point is needed.
results.modern_name: Parameter count for boundary value problems of analytic functions

results.what: Mixed boundary conditions: one equation per boundary point involving both u and v.
results.modern_name: Riemann–Hilbert problem (Hilbert's linear boundary problem, a·u + b·v = c on the boundary)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert 1904/05, who attributed the idea to Riemann's dissertation

results.what: Conjugation conditions: n boundary parts with associated points and n joint equations per n-tuple.
results.modern_name: Riemann boundary (conjugation/transmission) problem; germ of the Riemann monodromy problem
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (dissertation §19 and 1857 posthumous fragment); Hilbert, Plemelj, Noether, Gakhov, Muskhelishvili

results.what: Solvability and completeness may require finitely many additional or omitted constant conditions.
results.usually_credited_to: F. Noether 1921, Gakhov, Muskhelishvili (exact index formulas)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a draft of §17 of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation, and its content is essentially identical to the printed text. The anticipation of Riemann–Hilbert-type boundary problems in this section is well known and was acknowledged by Hilbert. The only novelty is draft wording variants such as the margin note on the arbitrary choice of v at one point.

checkable.sympy: x,y=symbols('x y',real=True); w=expand((x+I*y)**3); u=re(w); v=im(w); simplify(diff(u,x)-diff(v,y))==0 and simplify(diff(u,y)+diff(v,x))==0
checkable.asserts: Cauchy–Riemann equations hold for an analytic w, so the Art. 16 integrand vanishes for an analytic α+iβ.
The integrand of the Art. 16 functional is 0 for α+iβ = z² (expected output 0).
The real part of an analytic function is harmonic (output 0), which underlies uniqueness from boundary values of u.
Polar Cauchy–Riemann check (output 0): given u = Re z² on the unit circle, the conjugate v is fixed up to a constant, here pinned by v(0)=0.

checkable.sympy: x,y,c=symbols('x y c',real=True); v1=2*x*y; v2=2*x*y+c; simplify(diff(v2-v1,x))==0 and simplify(diff(v2-v1,y))==0
checkable.asserts: Two conjugates of the same u differ by a constant, which a single point value (condition 2) fixes.

transcription_corrections: 'dass {+a+} am Rande den gegebenen Werth gleich {+in der ganzen Fläche+} für jede...' should read 'dass a am Rande dem gegebenen Werthe gleich und in der ganzen Fläche für jede unendlich kleine Ortsänderung die Änderung von a+bi unendlich klein von derselben Ordnung ist'.

Margin note to 2): the insertion above the deleted 'That' is more plausibly 'an sich' than 'nur bis', and 'die gewählte[?] soll nur für unnöthige' is better read as 'die gemachte soll nur hier unnöthige Weitläufigkeiten abschneiden'.
'oder für mehreren Theile' should be 'oder für mehrere Theile'.

'mit je einem {+n-1+} bestimmten Punkte aus den übrigen n-1 Theilen' should be 'mit je einem bestimmten Punkte aus jedem der übrigen n-1 Theile'. The interlinear 'n-1' insertion is misplaced, and the margin rewrite ('dieser Theil n-1 bestimmte Punkte, aus jedem der übrigen Theile einer, zugesellt sind') is the intended replacement.
The first margin addition ('mit der Lage dieses Punktes ihre Form stetig ändernde') belongs before 'Gleichung' in 'Eine beide Glieder enthaltende Gleichung'.
The insertion in line 3 above 'Grösse' is 'complexen' (cf. published title 'veränderlichen complexen Grösse').
